title: dedicated-pool-warmup-thrash-notes
content:
Context:
This is my personal debugging scratchpad for the Dedicated GPU pool autoscaling incident we've been tracking — symptoms were repeated capacity thrash and prolonged cold-start/warmup latency for new nodes (esp. V100 pools). I captured commands run, log excerpts, quick experiments, and hypotheses. Not polished — notes to self and for Samira/Miguel to review.

Incident summary (user-facing impact):
- Time window: 2025-01-10 02:10 -> 2025-01-10 06:30 UTC (recurring over weekend batches)
- Symptoms: high request latencies (p95 > 2x SLO), token throughput drops, queue backlog spikes, autoscaler oscillating between adding 2–4 nodes and removing them within ~6–10 minutes.
- Affected: dedicated-pool:gpu-v100-8x (tenant: acme-retail-prod), drain/failover triggered for some routes.

Chronology / breadcrumbs:
- 2025-01-09 23:40 local: manual rollout of model v3.1 -> traffic shift 20% to dedicated pool for warmup testing.
- 2025-01-10 02:12 UTC: alert: pool CPU/GPU utilization falling then spiking, autoscale add node.
- 02:18 UTC: new node attached but remained UNREADY for ~4m30s (kube readiness failed: init kubelet-attach timeout).
- 02:24 UTC: autoscaler removed the node (scale down) due to perceived under-utilization, while still processing backlog -> thrash.
- 02:30-03:00: repeated add/remove cycle 3x.
- 03:15: started collecting detailed logs and increased logging level for serving runtime.

Commands tried (notes + outputs):
1) List pods and node statuses (ran during incident)
$ kubectl get pods -n serving --selector=pool=gpu-v100-8x -o wide
# output snippet
POD                                      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE    NODE
serve-abc-5z2k                            1/1     Running   0          55m    gpu-node-22
serve-abc-6xz1                            0/1     Pending   0          4m     <none>

$ kubectl describe pod serve-abc-6xz1 -n serving
Events:
  Type    Reason     Age    From               Message
  ----    ------     ----   ----               -------
  Warning Failed     4m     kubelet            Failed mount volume "nv-host-devices"
  Normal  Scheduled  4m     default-scheduler  Successfully assigned serving/serve-abc-6xz1 to gpu-node-24

Observation: Pending pods often showed mount/permission errors for NVidia host devices or driver not yet ready.

2) Check node GPU driver readiness
$ kubectl get nodes -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, gpu_plugin: .status.conditions[]? | select(.type=="KubeletReady")}'
# manual check: some nodes reported Ready=false for Kubelet for 30-90s after attach (likely driver init).

3) Autoscaler logs (scaledown events)
$ kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/cluster-autoscaler -f | grep "scaleDown" -n
# lines showed: scaleDown: Node gpu-node-24 had no more pods, removing. But there were pending pods in another AZ.

4) Simulate warmup with synthetic load to observe latency/warmup time
$ python tools/sim_load.py --pool gpu-v100-8x --concurrency 12 --duration 600
# observed 60–90s of high latency at start, then steadying. Re-run with --pin-cache True reduced latency start by ~30s.

Log excerpts (serving runtime):
[2025-01-10T02:14:20Z] WARN  warmup: model_load_time=24.7s, kv_init=11.2s
[2025-01-10T02:16:50Z] ERROR scheduler: unable to schedule request: no ready instances in pool gpu-v100-8x
[2025-01-10T02:20:05Z] INFO  autoscaler: scale_up recommended=2 -> starting attach; attach_id=att-0a1b2c
[2025-01-10T02:22:47Z] WARN  node-init: driver-check failed (nvml not found) -> retry

Hypotheses (ranked rough):
- H1: Node warmup (driver + model prefetch) takes longer than autoscaler scale-down grace period, causing premature removal — net effect thrash.
- H2: Device plugin (NVIDIA) initialization sometimes fails for first attach (race with kubelet), causing pods to Pending and autoscaler to think capacity isn't used.
- H3: Scheduler/binpacking: pods are being scheduled across too many distinct nodes (low pod density), increasing the number of node attachments and cold-starts.
- H4: Prefetch/warmup not enabled for canary model rollout, so first requests are heavier (model weights + quant tables).

Quick experiments and results (notes):
- Experiment A: Increase autoscaler --scale-down-unneeded-time from 5m to 12m for this pool only (config patch). Result: thrash frequency dropped, but cost increased; still saw high initial latency for the first 30–60s after node attach. (Good signal H1 partly true.)
- Experiment B: Node bootstrap tweak: add a 45s init container that waits for /dev/nvidia0 presence before marking Ready. Result: pending -> running transitions stabilized; attach failures reduced by ~70% across 10 trials. (Supports H2.)
- Experiment C: Scheduler hinting: updated PodTopolgySpread/affinity to prefer packing onto existing nodes when CPU/GPU available. Result: Lowered number of nodes used per pool (avg nodes dropped from 6->4 for same load), warmup stalls less frequent. (Supports H3.)
- Experiment D: Pre-warm model cache during node bootstrap (background load of model artifact to local disk and run a dummy generate to populate KV cache). Result: reduced model_load_time from ~25s -> ~6s and reduced observed p95 by ~40% for new nodes. (Supports H4 strongly.)

Failed attempts / red herrings:
- Flipping driver version to latest nightly (in a small test) added instability — revert.
- Disabling node autoscale entirely for the pool mitigated thrash but unacceptable for cost.

Actionable next steps (prioritized):
1) Short-term (hours):
   - Roll out node bootstrap change (init container waiting for /dev/nvidia* and nvml availability) to gpu-v100-8x pools. (Patch in PR #982)
   - Increase scale-down grace window to 10m for pools running canary traffic while we monitor.
   - Enable model prefetch/warmup on node attach (background job that warms weights + kv cache); feature flagged.

2) Medium-term (days):
   - Add autoscaler hooks to detect 'recently attached but failing device plugin' and treat as weighted capacity (prevent immediate scale-down).
   - Improve scheduler packing heuristics for GPU pools (prefer same-node placement when kernels and memory allow).
   - Add synthetic warmup load in rollout pipeline when shifting traffic to new model version.

3) Long-term (weeks):
   - Investigate faster driver initialization (collab with infra + NVIDIA) and consider baked AMIs with preloaded drivers and kubelet configs.
   - Cost analysis for keeping a small always-warm buffer (1–2 nodes) for high-SLA customers vs per-request cold start cost.

Notes to reviewer:
- The bootstrap init container is deliberately conservative (waits up to 60s) — needs review for failure modes.
- When we enabled prefetch on test nodes, we noticed an extra 2GB disk usage per model — watch eviction thresholds.
- Link to PR/patch: GitHub: redwood-inference/serving-runtime#982 (warmup boothook + init container)

Immediate log references / timestamps to include in incident ticket:
- 2025-01-10T02:12:07Z autoscaler saw scaleUpRecommended=2 (att-0a1b2c)
- 2025-01-10T02:16:37Z node-init error nvml not found (gpu-node-24)
- 2025-01-10T02:22:57Z scaleDown event removed gpu-node-24 while pods Pending existed

Open questions / unknowns:
- Are there specific AZs or instance launch paths that have higher attach latency? Need correlation with cloud provider events/logs.
- For very large models (>20B), is the prefetch approach sufficient or will we still see long kv_init times?
- Does current quota/placement logic cause scheduled pods to spread across nodes instead of packing? Need simulation.

References & context links:
- JIRA INF-1284 (incident case), PR #982, Slack thread in #infra-ops (link above).

TL;DR: Root cause appears to be combination of slower-than-expected node warmup (drivers + model prefetch) and aggressive autoscaler scale-down settings, amplified by scheduling spreading. Short-term mitigations (init container wait + bump scale-down window + prefetch) materially reduced thrash in tests. Next: push those patches selectively and instrument more metrics (node attach latency, device-plugin init time, model load time) to verify in prod.

-- Alex (notes, 2025-01-18)
